entries.63c67f87992f5c7679bbd2b1b9a432a01482e51c: <div sID="gen2310" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Lev.7" sID="Lev.7"/> <div eID="gen2310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2311" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2312" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The law of the trespass-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.1-Lev.7.7">ver. 1-7</reference>), with some further directions concerning the burnt-offering and the meat-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.8-Lev.7.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. II. The law of the peace-offering. The eating of it (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.11-Lev.7.21">ver. 11-21</reference>), on which occasion the prohibition of eating fat or blood is repeated (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.22-Lev.7.27">ver. 22-27</reference>), and the priests' share of it, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.28-Lev.7.34">ver. 28-34</reference>. III. The conclusion of those institutions, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.35-Lev.7.38">ver. 35</reference>, &c.
entries.145948d83e9d1c8e0f6a4dc900ce92d3cc6df46d: <div eID="gen2312" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2311" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Law of the Trespass-Offering. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2313" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Likewise this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the trespass offering: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> most holy. <hi type="super">2</hi> In the place where they kill the burnt offering shall they kill the trespass offering: and the blood thereof shall he sprinkle round about upon the altar. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he shall offer of it all the fat thereof; the rump, and the fat that covereth the inwards, <hi type="super">4</hi> And the two kidneys, and the fat that <hi type="italic">is</hi> on them, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the flanks, and the caul <hi type="italic">that is</hi> above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away: <hi type="super">5</hi> And the priest shall burn them upon the altar <hi type="italic">for</hi> an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a trespass offering. <hi type="super">6</hi> Every male among the priests shall eat thereof: it shall be eaten in the holy place: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> most holy. <hi type="super">7</hi> As the sin offering <hi type="italic">is,</hi> so <hi type="italic">is</hi> the trespass offering: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> one law for them: the priest that maketh atonement therewith shall have <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> And the priest that offereth any man's burnt offering, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the priest shall have to himself the skin of the burnt offering which he hath offered. <hi type="super">9</hi> And all the meat offering that is baken in the oven, and all that is dressed in the fryingpan, and in the pan, shall be the priest's that offereth it. <hi type="super">10</hi> And every meat offering, mingled with oil, and dry, shall all the sons of Aaron have, one <hi type="italic">as much</hi> as another. <div eID="gen2313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2314" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. Concerning the trespass-offering, that, being much of the same nature with the sin-offering, it was to be governed by the same rules, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.6">v. 6</reference>. When the blood and fat were offered to God to make atonement, the priests were to eat the flesh, as that of the sin-offering, in the holy place. The Jews have a tradition (as we have it from the learned bishop Patrick) concerning the sprinkling of the blood of the trespass-offering <hi type="italic">round about upon the altar,</hi> "That there was a scarlet line which went round about the altar exactly in the middle, and the blood of the burnt-offerings was sprinkled round about above the line, but that of the trespass-offerings and peace-offerings round about below the line." As to the flesh of the trespass-offering, the right to it belonged to the priest that offered it, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.7">v. 7</reference>. He that did the work must have the wages. This was an encouragement to the priests to give diligent attendance on the altar; the more ready and busy they were the more they got. Note, The more diligent we are in the services of religion the more we shall reap of the advantages of it. But any of the priests, and the males of their families, might be invited by him to whom it belonged to partake with him: <hi type="italic">Every male among the priests shall eat thereof,</hi> that is, may eat thereof, <hi type="italic">in the holy place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.7.6">v. 6</reference>. And, no doubt, it was the usage to treat one another with those perquisites of their office, by which friendship and fellowship were kept up among the priests. Freely they had received, and must freely give. It seems the offerer was not himself to have any share of his trespass-offering, as he was to have of his peace-offering; but it was all divided between the altar and the priest. They offered peace-offerings in thankfulness for mercy, and then it was proper to feast; but they offered trespass-offerings in sorrow for sin, and then fasting was more proper, in token of holy mourning, and a resolution to abstain from sin. 2. Concerning the burnt-offering it is here appointed that the priest that offered it should have the skin (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.8">v. 8</reference>), which no doubt he might make money of. "This" (the Jews say) "is meant only for the burnt-offerings which were offered by particular persons; for the profit of the skins of the daily burnt-offerings for the congregation went to the repair of the sanctuary." Some suggest that this appointment will help us to understand God's clothing our first parents with <hi type="italic">coats of skins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.3.21">Gen. iii. 21</reference>. It is probable that the beasts whose skins they were were offered in sacrifice as whole burnt-offerings, and that Adam was the priest that offered them; and then God gave him the skins, as his fee, to make clothes of for himself and his wife, in remembrance of which the skins ever after pertained to the priest; and see <reference osisRef="Gen.27.16">Gen. xxvii. 16</reference>. 3. Concerning the meat-offering, if it was dressed, it was fit to be eaten immediately; and therefore the priest that offered it was to have it, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.9">v. 9</reference>. If it was dry, there was not so much occasion for being in haste to use it; and therefore an equal dividend of it must be made among all the priests that were then in waiting, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.10">v. 10</reference>.
entries.9c7877232ca243c1441e7096891793a6e4697127: <div eID="gen2314" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Law of the Peace-Offering. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings, which he shall offer unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> If he offer it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving unleavened cakes mingled with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and cakes mingled with oil, of fine flour, fried. <hi type="super">13</hi> Besides the cakes, he shall offer <hi type="italic">for</hi> his offering leavened bread with the sacrifice of thanksgiving of his peace offerings. <hi type="super">14</hi> And of it he shall offer one out of the whole oblation <hi type="italic">for</hi> an heave offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">and</hi> it shall be the priest's that sprinkleth the blood of the peace offerings. 15 And the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten the same day that it is offered; he shall not leave any of it until the morning. <hi type="super">16</hi> But if the sacrifice of his offering <hi type="italic">be</hi> a vow, or a voluntary offering, it shall be eaten the same day that he offereth his sacrifice: and on the morrow also the remainder of it shall be eaten: <hi type="super">17</hi> But the remainder of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burnt with fire. <hi type="super">18</hi> And if <hi type="italic">any</hi> of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings be eaten at all on the third day, it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be imputed unto him that offereth it: it shall be an abomination, and the soul that eateth of it shall bear his iniquity. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the flesh that toucheth any unclean <hi type="italic">thing</hi> shall not be eaten; it shall be burnt with fire: and as for the flesh, all that be clean shall eat thereof. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the soul that eateth <hi type="italic">of</hi> the flesh of the sacrifice of peace offerings, that <hi type="italic">pertain</hi> unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , having his uncleanness upon him, even that soul shall be cut off from his people. <hi type="super">21</hi> Moreover the soul that shall touch any unclean <hi type="italic">thing, as</hi> the uncleanness of man, or <hi type="italic">any</hi> unclean beast, or any abominable unclean <hi type="italic">thing,</hi> and eat of the flesh of the sacrifice of peace offerings, which <hi type="italic">pertain</hi> unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , even that soul shall be cut off from his people. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">23</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, Ye shall eat no manner of fat, of ox, or of sheep, or of goat. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the fat of the beast that dieth of itself, and the fat of that which is torn with beasts, may be used in any other use: but ye shall in no wise eat of it. <hi type="super">25</hi> For whosoever eateth the fat of the beast, of which men offer an offering made by fire unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , even the soul that eateth <hi type="italic">it</hi> shall be cut off from his people. <hi type="super">26</hi> Moreover ye shall eat no manner of blood, <hi type="italic">whether it be</hi> of fowl or of beast, in any of your dwellings. <hi type="super">27</hi> Whatsoever soul <hi type="italic">it be</hi> that eateth any manner of blood, even that soul shall be cut off from his people. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">29</hi> Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, He that offereth the sacrifice of his peace offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall bring his oblation unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of the sacrifice of his peace offerings. 30 His own hands shall bring the offerings of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made by fire, the fat with the breast, it shall he bring, that the breast may be waved <hi type="italic">for</hi> a wave offering before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 31 And the priest shall burn the fat upon the altar: but the breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the right shoulder shall ye give unto the priest <hi type="italic">for</hi> an heave offering of the sacrifices of your peace offerings. <hi type="super">33</hi> He among the sons of Aaron, that offereth the blood of the peace offerings, and the fat, shall have the right shoulder for <hi type="italic">his</hi> part. <hi type="super">34</hi> For the wave breast and the heave shoulder have I taken of the children of Israel from off the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them unto Aaron the priest and unto his sons by a statute for ever from among the children of Israel. <div eID="gen2315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2316" type="x-p"/> All this relates to the peace-offerings: it is the repetition and explication of what we had before, with various additions. <div eID="gen2316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2317" type="x-p"/> I. The nature and intention of the peace-offerings are here more distinctly opened. They were offered either, 1. In thankfulness for some special mercy received, such as recovery from sickness, preservation in a journey, deliverance at sea, redemption out of captivity, all which are specified in <reference osisRef="Ps.107.1-Ps.107.43">Ps. cvii.</reference>, and for them men are called upon to offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.22">v. 22</reference>. Or, 2. In performance of some vow which a man made when he was in distress (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">v. 16</reference>), and this was less honourable than the former, though the omission of it would have been more culpable. Or, 3. In supplication for some special mercy which a man was in the pursuit and expectation of, here called a <hi type="italic">voluntary offering.</hi> This accompanied a man's prayers, as the former did his praises. We do not find that men were bound by the law, unless they had bound themselves by vow, to offer these peace-offerings upon such occasions, as they were to bring their sacrifices of atonement in case of sin committed. Not but that prayer and praise are as much our duty as repentance is; but here, in the expressions of their sense of mercy, God left them more to their liberty than in the expressions of their sense of sin—to try the generosity of their devotion, and that their sacrifices, being free-will offerings, might be the more laudable and acceptable; and, by obliging them to bring the sacrifices of atonement, God would show the necessity of the great propitiation. <div eID="gen2317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2318" type="x-p"/> II. The rites and ceremonies about the peace-offerings are enlarged upon. <div eID="gen2318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2319" type="x-p"/> 1. If the peace-offering was offered for a thanksgiving, a meat-offering must be offered with it, cakes of several sorts, and wafers (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">v. 12</reference>), and (which was peculiar to the peace-offerings) leavened bread must be offered, not to be burnt upon the altar, that was forbidden (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>), but to be eaten with the flesh of the sacrifice, that nothing might be wanting to make it a complete and pleasant feast; for unleavened bread was less grateful to the taste, and therefore, though enjoined in the passover for a particular reason, yet in other festivals leavened bread, which was lighter and more pleasant, was appointed, that men might feast at God's table as well as at their own. And some think that a meat-offering is required to be brought with every peace-offering, as well as with that of thanksgiving, by that law (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.29">v. 29</reference>) which requires an oblation with it, that the table might be as well furnished as the altar. <div eID="gen2319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2320" type="x-p"/> 2. The flesh of the peace-offerings, both that which was the priest's share and that which was the offerer's must be eaten quickly, and not kept long, either raw, or dressed, cold. If it was a peace-offering for thanksgiving, it must be all eaten the same day (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">v. 16</reference>); if a vow, or voluntary offering, it must be eaten either the same day or the day after, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">v. 16</reference>. If any was left beyond the time limited, it was to be burnt (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.17">v. 17</reference>); and, if any person ate of what was so left their conduct should be animadverted upon as a very high misdemeanour, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.18">v. 18</reference>. Though they were not obliged to eat it in the holy place, as those offerings that are called most holy, but might take it to their own tents and feast upon it there, yet God would by this law make them to know a difference between that and other meat, and religiously to observe it, that whereas they might keep other meat cold in the house as long as they thought fit, and warm it again if they pleased, and eat it three or four days after, they might not do so with the flesh of their peace-offerings, but it must be eaten immediately. (1.) Because God would not have that holy flesh to be in danger of putrefying, or being fly-blown, to prevent which it must be salted with <hi type="italic">fire</hi> (as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.49">Mark ix. 49</reference>) if it were kept; as, if it was used, it must be salted with salt. (2.) Because God would not have his people to be niggardly and sparing, and distrustful of providence, but cheerfully to enjoy what God gives them (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">Eccl. viii. 15</reference>), and to do good with it, and not to be anxiously solicitous for the morrow. (3.) The flesh of the peace-offerings was God's treat, and therefore God would have the disposal of it; and he orders it to be used generously for the entertainment of their friends, and charitably for the relief of the poor, to show that he is a bountiful benefactor, <hi type="italic">giving us all things richly to enjoy,</hi> the bread of the day in its day. If the sacrifice was thanksgiving, they were especially obliged thus to testify their holy joy in God's goodness by their holy feasting. This law is made very strict (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.18">v. 18</reference>), that if the offerer did not take care to have all his offering eaten by himself or his family, his friends or the poor, within the time limited by the law, or, in the event of any part being left, to burn it (which was the most decent way of disposing of it, the sacrifices upon the altar being <hi type="italic">consumed by fire</hi>), then his offering should not be accepted, nor imputed to him. Note, All the benefit of our religious services is lost if we do not improve them, and conduct ourselves aright afterwards. They are not acceptable to God if they have not a due influence upon ourselves. If a man seemed generous in bringing a peace-offering, and yet afterwards proved sneaking and paltry in the using of it, it was as if he had never brought it; nay, <hi type="italic">it shall be an abomination.</hi> Note, There is no mean between God's acceptance and his abhorrence. If our persons and performances are sincere and upright, they are accepted; if not, they are an abomination, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Prov. xv. 8</reference>. He that eats it after the time appointed shall <hi type="italic">bear his iniquity,</hi> that is, he shall be <hi type="italic">cut off from his people,</hi> as it is explained (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.8">ch. xix. 8</reference>), where this law is repeated. This law of eating the peace-offerings before the third day, that they might not putrefy, is applicable tot the resurrection of Christ after two days, that, being God's <hi type="italic">holy one,</hi> he might not see corruption, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Ps. xvi. 10</reference>. And some think that it instructs us speedily, and without delay, to partake of Christ and his grace, feeding and feasting thereon by faith to-day, <hi type="italic">while it is called to-day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.13-Heb.3.14">Heb. iii. 13, 14</reference>), for it will be too late shortly. <div eID="gen2320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2321" type="x-p"/> 3. But the flesh, and those that eat it, must be pure. (1.) The flesh must <hi type="italic">touch no unclean thing;</hi> if it did, it must not be eaten, but burnt, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.19">v. 19</reference>. If, in carrying it from the altar to the place where it was eaten, a dog touched it, or it touched a dead body or any other unclean thing, it was then unfit to be used in a religious feast. Every thing we honour the holy God with must be pure and carefully kept from all pollution. It is a case adjudged (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.12">Hag. ii. 12</reference>) that the holy flesh could not by its touch communicate holiness to what was common; but by this law it is determined that by the touch of that which was unclean it received pollution from it, which intimates that the infection of sin is more easily and more frequently communicated than the savour of grace. (2.) It must not be eaten by any unclean person. When a person was upon any account ceremonially unclean it was at his peril if he presumed to eat of the flesh of the peace-offerings, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.20-Lev.7.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. Holy things are only for holy persons; the holiness of the food being ceremonial, those were incapacitated to partake of it who lay under any ceremonial uncleanness; but we are hereby taught to preserve ourselves pure from all the pollutions of sin, that we may have the benefit and comfort of Christ's sacrifice, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.1-1Pet.2.2">1 Pet. ii. 1, 2</reference>. Our consciences must be purged from dead works, that we may be fit to <hi type="italic">serve the living God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">Heb. ix. 14</reference>. But if any dare to partake of the table of the Lord under the pollution of sin unrepented of, and so profane sacred things, they eat and drink <hi type="italic">judgment to themselves,</hi> as those did that ate of the peace-offerings (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.20">v. 20</reference>) and again (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.21">v. 21</reference>), that they <hi type="italic">pertain unto the Lord:</hi> whatever pertains to the Lord is sacred, and must be used with great reverence and not with unhallowed hands. "<hi type="italic">Be you holy,</hi> for God is holy, and you pertain to him." <div eID="gen2321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2322" type="x-p"/> 4. The eating of blood and the fat of the inwards is here again prohibited; and the prohibition is annexed as before to the law of the peace-offerings, <reference osisRef="Lev.3.17">ch. iii. 17</reference>. (1.) The prohibition of the fat seems to be confined to those beasts which were used for sacrifice, the bullocks, sheep, and goats: but of the roe-buck, the hart, and other clean beasts, they might eat the fat; for those only of which offerings were brought are mentioned here, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.23-Lev.7.25">v. 23-25</reference>. This was to preserve in their minds a reverence for God's altar, on which the fat of the inwards was burnt. The Jews say, "If a man eat so much as an olive of forbidden fat—if he do it presumptuously, he is in danger of being cut off by the hand of God—if ignorantly, he is to bring a sin-offering, and so to pay dearly for his carelessness." To eat of the flesh of that which died of itself, or was torn of beasts, was unlawful; but to eat of the fat of such was doubly unlawful, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.24">v. 24</reference>. (2.) The prohibition of blood is more general (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.26-Lev.7.27">v. 26, 27</reference>), because the fat was offered to God only by way of acknowledgment, but the blood <hi type="italic">made atonement for the soul,</hi> and so typified Christ's sacrifice much more than the burning of the fat did; to this therefore a greater reverence must be paid, till these types had their accomplishment in the offering up of the body of Christ once for all. The Jews rightly expound this law as forbidding only the <hi type="italic">blood of the life,</hi> as they express it, not that which we call the <hi type="italic">gravy,</hi> for of that they supposed it was lawful to eat. <div eID="gen2322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2323" type="x-p"/> 5. The priest's share of the peace-offerings is here prescribed. Out of every beast that was offered for a peace-offering the priest that offered it was to have to himself the breast and the right shoulder, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.30-Lev.7.34">v. 30-34</reference>. Observe here, (1.) That when the sacrifice was killed the offerer himself must, with his own hands, present God's part of it, that he might signify thereby his cheerfully giving it up to God, and his desire that it might be accepted. He was with his own hands to <hi type="italic">lift it up,</hi> in token of his regard to God as the God of heaven, and then to <hi type="italic">wave it to and fro,</hi> in token of his regard to God as the Lord of the whole earth, to whom thus, as far as he could reach, he offered it, showing his readiness and wish to do him honour. Now that which was thus heaved and waved was the fat, and the breast, and the right shoulder, it was all offered to God; and then he ordered the fat to his altar, and the breast and shoulder to his priest, both being his receivers. (2.) That when the fat was burnt the priest took his part, on which he and his family were to feast, as well as the offerer and his family. In holy joy and thanksgiving, it is good to have our ministers to go before us, and to be our mouth to God. The melody is sweet when he that sows and those that reap rejoice together. Some observe a significancy in the parts assigned to the priests: the breast and the shoulder intimate the affections and the actions, which must be devoted to the honour of God by all his people and to the service also of the church by all his priests. Christ, our great peace-offering, feasts all his spiritual priests with the breast and shoulder, with the dearest love and the sweetest and strongest supports; for his is the wisdom of God and the power of God. When Saul was designed for a king Samuel ordered the shoulder of the peace-offering to be set before him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.24">1 Sam. ix. 24</reference>), which gave him a hint of something great and sacred intended for him. Jesus Christ is our great peace-offering; for he made himself a sacrifice, not only to atone for sin, and so to save us from the curse, but to purchase a blessing for us, and all good. By our joyfully partaking of the benefits of redemption we <hi type="italic">feast upon the sacrifice,</hi> to signify which the Lord's supper was instituted.
entries.e00fb74f4a6d77d9a589800451d2a256e2772820: <div eID="gen2323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2324" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> This <hi type="italic">is the portion</hi> of the anointing of Aaron, and of the anointing of his sons, out of the offerings of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made by fire, in the day <hi type="italic">when</hi> he presented them to minister unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the priest's office; 36 Which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded to be given them of the children of Israel, in the day that he anointed them, <hi type="italic">by</hi> a statute for ever throughout their generations. 37 This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the burnt offering, of the meat offering, and of the sin offering, and of the trespass offering, and of the consecrations, and of the sacrifice of the peace offerings; 38 Which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses in Mount Sinai, in the day that he commanded the children of Israel to offer their oblations unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , in the wilderness of Sinai. <div eID="gen2324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2325" type="x-p"/> Here is the conclusion of these laws concerning the sacrifices, though some of them are afterwards repeated and explained. These are to be considered, 1. As a grant to the priests, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.35-Lev.7.36">v. 35, 36</reference>. In the day they were ordained to that work and office this provision was made for their comfortable maintenance. Note, God will take care that those who are employed for him be well paid and well provided for. Those that receive the anointing of the Spirit to minister unto the Lord shall have their portion, and it shall be a worthy portion, out of the offerings of the Lord; for God's work is its own wages, and there is a present reward of obedience in obedience. 2. As a statute for ever to the people, that they should bring these offerings according to the rules prescribed, and cheerfully give the priests their share out of them. God <hi type="italic">commanded the children of Israel to offer their oblations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">v. 38</reference>. Note, The solemn acts religious worship are commanded. They are not things that we are left to our liberty in, and which we may do or not do at our pleasure; but we are under indispensable obligations to perform them in their season, and it is at our peril if we omit them. The observance of the laws of Christ cannot be less necessary than the observance of the laws of Moses was.  <chapter eID="Lev.7"/> <div eID="gen2325" type="x-p"/>

entries.aed46028e60174f8f6b3e1c6c0d597be6b43736d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1026"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.7.1-Lev.7.27">Le 7:1-27</reference>. The Law of the Trespass Offering.</title> <div sID="gen1416" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1026"/><hi type="bold">1. Likewise this is the law of the trespass offering--</hi>This chapter is a continuation of the laws that were to regulate the duty of the priests respecting the trespass offerings. The same regulations obtained in this case as in the burnt offerings--part was to be consumed on the altar, while the other part was a perquisite of the priests--some fell exclusively to the officiating minister, and was the fee for his services; others were the common share of all the priestly order, who lived upon them as their provision, and whose meetings at a common table would tend to promote brotherly harmony and friendship. <div eID="gen1416" type="x-p"/>
entries.23f62e80a0948b06c47e347fae8b3a98d1d897b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1027"/><div sID="gen1417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1027"/><hi type="bold">8. the priest shall have to himself the skin of the burnt offering which he hath offered--</hi>All the flesh and the fat of the burnt offerings being consumed, nothing remained to the priest but the skin. It has been thought that this was a patriarchal usage, incorporated with the Mosaic law, and that the right of the sacrificer to the skin of the victim was transmitted from the example of Adam (see on <reference osisRef="Gen.3.21">Ge 3:21</reference>). <div eID="gen1417" type="x-p"/>
entries.35e859e47ac350b0e9a2e44336be1d583f9ebb6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1028"/><div sID="gen1418" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1028"/><hi type="bold">11-14. this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings--</hi>Besides the usual accompaniments of other sacrifices, leavened bread was offered with the peace offerings, as a thanksgiving, such bread being common at feasts. <div eID="gen1418" type="x-p"/>
entries.b609adebdc2ec7320b68892d063d2fa1860e28d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1029"/><div sID="gen1419" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1029"/><hi type="bold">15-17. the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings ... shall be eaten the same day that it is offered--</hi>The flesh of the sacrifices was eaten on the day of the offering or on the day following. But if any part of it remained till the third day, it was, instead of being made use of, to be burned with fire. In the East, butcher-meat is generally eaten the day it is killed, and it is rarely kept a second day, so that as a prohibition was issued against any of the flesh in the peace offerings being used on the third day, it has been thought, not without reason, that this injunction must have been given to prevent a superstitious notion arising that there was some virtue or holiness belonging to it. <div eID="gen1419" type="x-p"/>
entries.77b26715a63e68aa05d6d820fccb21a0cc655bae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1030"/><div sID="gen1420" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1030"/><hi type="bold">18. if any of the flesh of the sacrifice ... be eaten at all on the third day, it shall not be accepted, neither ... imputed--</hi>The sacrifice will not be acceptable to God nor profitable to him that offers it. <div eID="gen1420" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3fd6f4188fa49adcae5a17d85394e2b5f7077b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1031"/><div sID="gen1421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1031"/><hi type="bold">20. cut off from his people--</hi>that is, excluded from the privileges of an Israelite--lie under a sentence of excommunication. <div eID="gen1421" type="x-p"/>
entries.5102446a6e906936905d26ec83643d534578aa66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1032"/><div sID="gen1422" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1032"/><hi type="bold">21. abominable unclean thing--</hi>Some copies of the Bible read, "any reptile." <div eID="gen1422" type="x-p"/>
entries.6efeb186546f87582da56ee3e4f6de78dd7b899a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1033"/><div sID="gen1423" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1033"/><hi type="bold">22-27. Ye shall eat no manner of fat--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Lev.3.17">Le 3:17</reference>). <div eID="gen1423" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc4f752a0178dff5519968ea7fb8e1015280ce9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1034"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lev.7.28-Lev.7.38">Le 7:28-38</reference>. The Priests' Portion.</title> <div sID="gen1424" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1034"/><hi type="bold">29-34. He that offereth the sacrifice of his peace offerings unto the Lord--</hi>In order to show that the sacrifice was voluntary, the offerer was required to bring it with his own hands to the priest. The breast having been waved to and fro in a solemn manner as devoted to God, was given to the priests; it was assigned to the use of their order generally, but the right shoulder was the perquisite of the officiating priest. <div eID="gen1424" type="x-p"/>
entries.a10712fbf35ad80c749a2e7ecba047e43165c96f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1035"/><div sID="gen1425" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1035"/><hi type="bold">35-38. This is the portion of the anointing of Aaron--</hi>These verses contain a general summing up of the laws which regulate the privileges and duties of the priests. The word "anointing" is often used as synonymous with "office" or "dignity." So that the "portion of the anointing of Aaron" probably means the provision made for the maintenance of the high priest and the numerous body of functionaries which composed the sacerdotal order.<div eID="gen1425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the day when he presented them to minister unto the Lord, &c.--</hi>that is, from the day they approached the Lord in the duties of their ministry. <chapter eID="Lev.7"/>

entries.0a01000a0722db8a079ead64bf0007edf6f563b1: <div eID="gen4392" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4393" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4394" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4394" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4393" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4395" type="x-p"/> The law of the trespass-offering, and the priest's portion in it, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.1-Lev.7.7">Lev 7:1-7</reference>. As also in the sin-offerings and meat-offerings, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.8-Lev.7.10">Lev 7:8-10</reference>. The law of the sacrifice of peace-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.11">Lev 7:11</reference>, whether it was a thanksgiving - offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.12-Lev.7.15">Lev 7:12-15</reference>; or a Vow or voluntary offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16-Lev.7.18">Lev 7:16-18</reference>. Concerning the flesh that touched any unclean thing, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.19">Lev 7:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.20">Lev 7:20</reference>, and the person who touched any thing unclean, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.21">Lev 7:21</reference>. Laws concerning eating of fat, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.22-Lev.7.25">Lev 7:22-25</reference>, and concerning eating of blood, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.26">Lev 7:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.27">Lev 7:27</reference>. Farther ordinances concerning the peace-offerings and the priest's portion in them, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.28-Lev.7.36">Lev 7:28-36</reference>. Conclusion of the laws and ordinances relative to burnt-offerings, meat-offerings, sin-offerings, and peace-offerings, delivered in this and the preceding chapters, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.37">Lev 7:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">Lev 7:38</reference>. <div eID="gen4395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4396" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen4396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4397" type="x-p"/> Trespass-offering - See end of the chapter at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">Lev 7:38</reference> (note).
entries.89c86b3e4375ebe0a683b7e459924efdbef84d0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen4397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4398" type="x-p"/> In the place where they kill the burnt-offering - viz., on the north side of the altar, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.11">Lev 1:11</reference>.
entries.e0a497de14138b5503fea8fd6e41ea73410438e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen4398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4399" type="x-p"/> The rump - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.3.9">Lev 3:9</reference>, where the principal subjects in this chapter are explained, being nearly the same in both.
entries.2e7a1a01ca22b368c9cc68a19d471f1c6d47032d: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen4399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4400" type="x-p"/> The fat that is on them - Chiefly the fat that was found in a detached state, not mixed with the muscles; such as the omentum or caul, the fat of the mesentery, the fat about the kidneys, etc. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.3.9">Lev 3:9</reference>, etc.
entries.66cefc5e334c7d862cba527efb001dd172ceb26d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen4400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4401" type="x-p"/> The priest shall have to himself the skin - Bishop Patrick supposes that this right of the priest to the skin commenced with the offering of Adam, "for it is probable," says he, "that Adam himself offered the first sacrifice, and had the skin given him by God to make garments for him and his wife; in conformity to which the priests ever after had the skin of the whole burnt-offerings for their portion, which was a custom among the Gentiles as well as the Jews, who gave the skins of their sacrifices to their priests, when they were not burnt with the sacrifices, as in some sin-offerings they were among the Jews, see <reference osisRef="Lev.4.11">Lev 4:11</reference>. And they employed them to a superstitious use, by lying upon them in their temples, in hopes to have future things revealed to them in their dreams. <div eID="gen4401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4402" type="x-p"/> Of this we have a proof in Virgil, Aen. lib. vii., ver. 86-95. " - huc dona sacerdos <div eID="gen4402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4403" type="x-p"/> Cum tulit, et caesarum ovium sub nocte silenti <div eID="gen4403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4404" type="x-p"/> Pellibus incubuit stratis, somnosque petivit; <div eID="gen4404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4405" type="x-p"/> Multa modus simulncra videt volitantia miris, <div eID="gen4405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4406" type="x-p"/> Et varias audit voces, fruiturque deorum <div eID="gen4406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4407" type="x-p"/> Colloquio, atque imis Acheronta affatur Avernis. <div eID="gen4407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4408" type="x-p"/> Hic et tum pater ipse petens responsa Latinus <div eID="gen4408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4409" type="x-p"/> Centum lanigeras mactabat rite bidentes, <div eID="gen4409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4410" type="x-p"/> Atque harum effultus tergo stratisque jacebat <div eID="gen4410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4411" type="x-p"/> Velleribus. Subita ex alto vox reddita luco est." <div eID="gen4411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4412" type="x-p"/> First, on the fleeces of the slaughter'd sheep <div eID="gen4412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4413" type="x-p"/> By night the sacred priest dissolves in sleep, <div eID="gen4413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4414" type="x-p"/> When in a train, before his slumbering eye, <div eID="gen4414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4415" type="x-p"/> Thin airy forms and wondrous visions fly. <div eID="gen4415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4416" type="x-p"/> He calls the powers who guard the infernal floods, <div eID="gen4416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4417" type="x-p"/> And talks, inspired, familiar with the gods. <div eID="gen4417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4418" type="x-p"/> To this dread oracle the prince withdrew, <div eID="gen4418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4419" type="x-p"/> And first a hundred sheep the monarch slew; <div eID="gen4419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4420" type="x-p"/> Then on their fleeces lay; and from the wood <div eID="gen4420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4421" type="x-p"/> He heard, distinct, these accents of the god. - Pitt. <div eID="gen4421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4422" type="x-p"/> The same superstition, practiced precisely in the same way and for the same purposes, prevail to the present day in the Highlands of Scotland, as the reader may see from the following note of Sir Walter Scott, in his Lady of the Lake: - "The Highlanders of Scotland, like all rude people, had various superstitious modes of inquiring into futurity. One of the most noted was the togharm. A person was wrapped up in the skin of a newly-slain bullock, and deposited beside a water-fall, or at the bottom of a precipice, or in some other strange, wild, and unusual situation, where the scenery around him suggested nothing but objects of horror. In this situation he revolved in his mind the question proposed; and whatever was impressed upon him by his exalted imagination, passed for the inspiration of the disembodied spirits who haunt these desolate recesses. One way of consulting this oracle was by a party of men, who first retired to solitary places, remote from any house, and there they singled out one of their number, and wrapt him in a big cow's hide, which they folded about him; his whole body was covered with it except his head, and so left in this posture all night, until his invisible friends relieved him by giving a proper answer to the question in hand; which he received, as he fancied, from several persons that he found about him all that time. His consorts returned to him at day-break; and then he communicated his news to them, which often proved fatal to those concerned in such unwarrantable inquiries. "Mr. Alexander Cooper, present minister of North Virt, told me that one John Erach, in the Isle of Lewis, assured him it was his fate to have been led by his curiosity with some who consulted this oracle, and that he was a night within the hide above mentioned, during which time he felt and heard such terrible things that he could not express them: the impression made on him was such as could never go off; and he said, for a thousand worlds he would never again be concerned in the like performance, for it had disordered him to a high degree. He confessed it ingenuously, and with an air of great remorse, and seemed to be very penitent under a just sense of so great a crime: he declared this about five years since, and is still living in the Isle of Lewis for any thing I know." - Description of the Western Isles, p. 110. See also Pennant's Scottish Tour, vol. ii., p. 301; and Sir W. Scott's Lady of the Lake.
entries.814b3c6eda7474940b6ae35c0eb9811bf6845dba: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen4422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4423" type="x-p"/> Baken in the oven - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Lev.2.5">Lev 2:5</reference>, etc.
entries.1b61232e28aafbdb0335a619c47e5f069d9cbac7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen4423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4424" type="x-p"/> If he offer it for a thanksgiving - See the notes at the end of this chapter at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.38">Lev 7:38</reference> (note).
entries.ae321cc26669bcb94f61d32132abac367a0445ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen4424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4425" type="x-p"/> He shall not leave any of it until the morning - Because in such a hot country it was apt to putrefy, and as it was considered to be holy, it would have been very improper to expose that to putrefaction which had been consecrated to the Divine Being. Mr. Harmer supposes that the law here refers rather to the custom of drying flesh which had been devoted to religious purposes, which is practiced among the Mohammedans to the present time. This, he thinks, might have given rise to the prohibition, as the sacred flesh thus preserved might have been abused to superstitious purposes. Therefore God says, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.18">Lev 7:18</reference>, "If any of the flesh of the sacrifice - be eaten at all on the third day, it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be imputed unto him that offereth it; it is an abomination, and the soul that eateth of it shall bear his iniquity." That is, on Mr. Harmer's hypothesis, This sacred flesh shall avail nothing to him that eats it after the first or second day on which it is offered; however consecrated before, it shall not be considered sacred after that time. See Harmer's Obs., vol. i., p. 394, edit. 1808.
entries.65e118ea98c40b96afb2f24c155c023adb6d7a03: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen4425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4426" type="x-p"/> Having his uncleanness upon him - Having touched any unclean thing by which he became legally defiled, and had not washed his clothes, and bathed his flesh.
entries.66726f989b6ac27720925714266c10537d55a4b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen4426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4427" type="x-p"/> The uncleanness of man - Any ulcer, sore, or leprosy; or any sort of cutaneous disorder, either loathsome or infectious.
entries.7718074b00f45f6602b19c2da77ac2708bbe1c67: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen4427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4428" type="x-p"/> Fat, of ox, or of sheep, or of goat - Any other fat they might eat, but the fat of these was sacred, because they were the only animals which were offered in sacrifice, though many others ranked among the clean animals as well as these. But it is likely that this prohibition is to be understood of these animals when offered in sacrifice, and then only in reference to the inward fat, as mentioned on <reference osisRef="Lev.7.4">Lev 7:4</reference>. Of the fat in any other circumstances it cannot be intended, as it was one of the especial blessings which God gave to the people. Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with Fat of Lambs, and Rams of the breed of Bashan, and Goats, were the provision that he gave to his followers. See <reference osisRef="Deu.32.12-Deu.32.14">Deu 32:12-14</reference>.
entries.7db9c8d8fd7a0242c76c61d6939b4b11b269e909: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen4428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4429" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever soul - that eateth any manner of blood - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen 9:4</reference>. Shall be cut off - excommunicated from the people of God, and so deprived of any part in their inheritance, and in their blessings. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.17.14">Gen 17:14</reference>.
entries.70039c7c69ac365701e7325e48c17583e92bdfa2: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen4429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4430" type="x-p"/> Shall bring his oblation - Meaning those things which were given out of the peace-offerings to the Lord and to the priest - Ainsworth.
entries.a5880b4fe4a89621e5785baf21fd0c07d51f1cc3: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen4430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4431" type="x-p"/> Wave-offering - See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.27">Exo 29:27</reference> (note).
entries.d21f070c332a254fa6f35f8e8303d231d2f0abdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen4431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4432" type="x-p"/> The right shoulder - See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.27">Exo 29:27</reference> (note).
entries.4c7563c2c2cc96cbd34192dc7fe622223338b8dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen4432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4433" type="x-p"/> In the day that he anointed them - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.40.15">Exo 40:15</reference>.
entries.d3699516ad4c0962a261d8d0fe5cdf352e8b84ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen4433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4434" type="x-p"/> In the wilderness of Sinai - These laws were probably given to Moses while he was on the mount with God; the time was quite sufficient, as he was there with God not less than fourscore days in all; forty days at the giving, and forty days at the renewing of the law. As in the course of this book the different kinds of sacrifices commanded to be offered are repeatedly occurring, I think it best, once for all, to give a general account of them, and a definition of the original terms, as well as of all others relative to this subject which are used in the Old Testament, and the reference in which they all stood to the great sacrifice offered by Christ. <div eID="gen4434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4435" type="x-p"/> 1. אשם Asham, Trespass-offering, from אשם asham, to be guilty, or liable to punishment; for in this sacrifice the guilt was considered as being transferred to the animal offered up to God, and the offerer redeemed from the penalty of his sin, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.37">Lev 7:37</reference>. Christ is said to have made his soul an offering for sin, (אשם), <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa 53:10</reference>. <div eID="gen4435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4436" type="x-p"/> 2. אשה Ishsheh, Fire-offering, probably from אשש ashash, to be grieved, angered, inflamed; either pointing out the distressing nature of sin, or its property of incensing Divine justice against the offender, who, in consequence, deserving burning for his offense, made use of this sacrifice to be freed from the punishment due to his transgression. It occurs <reference osisRef="Exo.29.18">Exo 29:18</reference>, and in many places of this book. <div eID="gen4436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4437" type="x-p"/> 3. הבהבים Habhabim, Iterated Or Repeated offerings, from יהב yahab, to supply. The word occurs only in <reference osisRef="Hos.8.13">Hos 8:13</reference>, and probably means no more than the continual repetition of the accustomed offerings, or continuation of each part of the sacred service. <div eID="gen4437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4438" type="x-p"/> 4. זבח Zebach, A Sacrifice, (in Chaldee, דבח debach, the ז zain being changed into ד daleth), a creature slain in sacrifice, from זבח zabach, to slay; hence the altar on which such sacrifices were offered was termed מזבח mizbeach, the place of sacrifice. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.8.20">Gen 8:20</reference>. Zebach is a common name for sacrifices in general. <div eID="gen4438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4439" type="x-p"/> 5. חג Chag, a festival, especially such as had a periodical return, from חגג chagag, to celebrate a festival, to dance round and round in circles. See <reference osisRef="Exo.5.1">Exo 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.12.24">Exo 12:24</reference>. The circular dance was probably intended to point out the revolution of the heavenly bodies, and the exact return of the different seasons. See Parkhurst. <div eID="gen4439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4440" type="x-p"/> 6. חטאת Chattath and חטאה Chattaah, Sin-offering, from חטא chata, to miss the mark; it also signifies sin in general, and is a very apt term to express its nature by. A sinner is continually aiming at and seeking happiness; but as he does not seek it in God, hence the Scripture represents him as missing his aim, or missing the mark. This is precisely the meaning of the Greek word ἁμαρτια, translated sin and sin-offering in our version; and this is the term by which the Hebrew word is translated both by the Septuagint and the inspired writers of the New Testament. The sin-offering was at once an acknowledgment of guilt, in having forsaken the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns that could hold none; and also of the firm purpose of the offerer to return to God, the true and pure fountain of blessedness. This word often occurs. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference>. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.13.13">Gen 13:13</reference>. <div eID="gen4440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4441" type="x-p"/> 7. כפר Copher, the Expiation or Atonement, from כפר caphar, to cover, to smear over, or obliterate, or annul a contract. Used often to signify the atonement or expiation made for the pardon or cancelling of iniquity. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.25.17">Exo 25:17</reference>. <div eID="gen4441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4442" type="x-p"/> 8. מועד Moed, an Appointed annual festival, from יעד yaad, to appoint or constitute, signifying such feasts as were instituted in commemoration of some great event or deliverance, such as the deliverance from Egypt. See <reference osisRef="Exo.13.10">Exo 13:10</reference>, and thus differing from the chag mentioned above. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.1.14">Gen 1:14</reference>. <div eID="gen4442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4443" type="x-p"/> 9. מלאים Milluim, Consecrations or consecration-offerings, from מלא mala, to fill; those offerings made in consecrations, of which the priests partook, or, in the Hebrew phrase, had their hands filled, or which had filled the hands of them that offered them. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.19">Exo 29:19</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.9">2Chr 13:9</reference>. <div eID="gen4443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4444" type="x-p"/> 10. מנחה Minchah, Meat-offering, from נח nach, to rest, settle after toil. It generally consisted of things without life, such as green ears of corn, full ears of corn, flour, oil, and frankincense; (see on <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Lev 2:1</reference> (note), etc.); and may be considered as having its name from that rest from labor and toil which a man had when the fruits of the autumn were brought in, or when, in consequence of obtaining any rest, ease, etc., a significant offering or sacrifice was made to God. It often occurs. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.4.3">Gen 4:3</reference>. The jealousy-offering (<reference osisRef="Num.5.15">Num 5:15</reference>) was a simple minchah, consisting of barley-meal only. <div eID="gen4444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4445" type="x-p"/> 11. מסך Mesech and ממסך Mimsach, a Mixture-offering, or Mixed Libation, called a Drink-offering, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Isa 55:11</reference>, from מסך masach, to mingle; it seems in general to mean old wine mixed with the less, which made it extremely intoxicating. This offering does not appear to have had any place in the worship of the true God; but from <reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Isa 65:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Pro.23.30">Pro 23:30</reference>, it seems to have been used for idolatrous purposes, such as the Bacchanalia among the Greeks and Romans, "when all got drunk in honor of the god." <div eID="gen4445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4446" type="x-p"/> 12. משאת Masseeth, an Oblation, things carried to the temple to be presented to God, from נשא nasa, to bear or carry, to bear sin; typically, <reference osisRef="Exo.28.38">Exo 28:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.10.17">Lev 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.16.21">Lev 16:21</reference>; really, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Isa 53:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa 53:12</reference>. The sufferings and death of Christ were the true masseeth or vicarious bearing of the sins of mankind, as the passage in Isaiah above referred to sufficiently proves. See this alluded to by the Evangelist John, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference> (note); and see the root in Parkhurst. <div eID="gen4446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4447" type="x-p"/> 13. נדבה Nedabah, Free-Will, or voluntary offering; from נדב nadab, to be free, liberal, princely. An offering not commanded, but given as a particular proof of extraordinary gratitude to God for especial mercies, or on account of some vow or engagement voluntarily taken, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>. <div eID="gen4447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4448" type="x-p"/> 14. נסך Nesech, Libation, Or Drink-offering, from נסך nasach, to diffuse or pour out. Water or wine poured out at the conclusion or confirmation of a treaty or covenant. To this kind of offering there is frequent allusion and reference in the New Testament, as it typified the blood of Christ poured out for the sin of the world; and to this our Lord himself alludes in the institution of the holy eucharist. The whole Gospel economy is represented as a covenant or treaty between God and man, Jesus Christ being not only the mediator, but the covenant sacrifice, whose blood was poured out for the ratification and confirmation of this covenant or agreement between God and man. <div eID="gen4448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4449" type="x-p"/> 15. עלה and עולה Olah, Burnt-offering, from עלה alah, to ascend, because this offering, as being wholly consumed, ascended as it were to God in smoke and vapor. It was a very expressive type of the sacrifice of Christ, as nothing less than his complete and full sacrifice could make atonement for the sin of the world. In most other offerings the priest, and often the offerer, had a share, but in the whole burnt-offering all was given to God. <div eID="gen4449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4450" type="x-p"/> 16. קטרת Ketoreth, Incense Or Perfume-offering, from קטר katar, to burn, i. e., the frankincense, and other aromatics used as a perfume in different parts of the Divine service. To this St. Paul compares the agreeableness of the sacrifice of Christ to God, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Eph 5:2</reference> : Christ hath given himself for us, an offering - to God for a Sweet-Smelling savor. From <reference osisRef="Rev.5.8">Rev 5:8</reference> we learn that it was intended also to represent the prayers of the saints, which, offered up on the altar, Christ Jesus, that sanctifies every gift, are highly pleasing in the sight of God. <div eID="gen4450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4451" type="x-p"/> 17. קרבן Korban, the Gift-offering, from קרב karab to draw nigh or approach. See this explained on <reference osisRef="Lev.1.2">Lev 1:2</reference> (note). Korban was a general name for any kind of offering, because through these it was supposed a man had access to his Maker. <div eID="gen4451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4452" type="x-p"/> 18. שלמים Shelamim, Peace-offering, from שלם shalam, to complete, make whole; for by these offerings that which was lacking was considered as being now made up, and that which was broken, viz., the covenant of God, by his creatures' transgression, was supposed to be made whole; so that after such an offering, the sincere and conscientious mind had a right to consider that the breach was made up between God and it, and that it might lay confident hold on this covenant of peace. To this the apostle evidently alludes, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.19">Eph 2:14-19</reference> : He is our peace, (i. e. our shalam or peace-offering), who has made both one, and broken down the middle wall; having abolished in his flesh the enmity, etc. See the whole passage, and see Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Gen 14:18</reference>. <div eID="gen4452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4453" type="x-p"/> 19. תודה Todah, Thank-offering, from ידה yadah, to confess; offerings made to God with public confession of his power, goodness, mercy, etc. <div eID="gen4453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4454" type="x-p"/> 20. תנופה Tenuphah, Wave-offering, from נף naph, to stretch out; an offering of the first-fruits stretched out before God, in acknowledgment of his providential goodness. This offering was moved from the right hand to the left. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.27">Exo 29:27</reference>. <div eID="gen4454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4455" type="x-p"/> 21. תרומה Terumah, Heave-offering, from רם ram, to lift up, because the offering was lifted up towards heaven, as the wave - offering, in token of the kindness of God in granting rain and fruitful seasons, and filling the heart with food and gladness. As the wave-offering was moved from right to left, so the heave-offering was moved up and down; and in both cases this was done several times. These offerings had a blessed tendency to keep alive in the breasts of the people a due sense of their dependence on the Divine providence and bounty, and of their obligation to God for his continual and liberal supply of all their wants. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.27">Exo 29:27</reference>. <div eID="gen4455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4456" type="x-p"/> In the above collection are comprised, as far as I can recollect, an explanation of all the terms used in the Hebrew Scriptures which signify sacrifice, oblation, atonement, offering, etc., etc., as well as the reference they bear to the great and only sufficient atonement, sacrifice, oblation, and satisfaction made by Christ Jesus for the sins of mankind. Larger accounts must be sought in authors who treat professedly on these subjects.  <chapter eID="Lev.7"/> <div eID="gen4456" type="x-p"/>

entries.e8a8b9d462dcb1fac02870b9805dd6b687382103: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.1">Lev 7:1</reference> <div eID="gen1226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1227" type="x-p"/> The Law of the Trespass-Offering embraces first of all the regulations as to the ceremonial connected with the presentation.
entries.28d7737cdcde00f4e0bb51dce042a0d1a5d69891: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.2">Lev 7:2</reference> <div eID="gen1227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1228" type="x-p"/> The slaughtering and sprinkling of the blood were the same as in the case of the burnt-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.5">Lev 1:5</reference>); and therefore, no doubt, the signification was the same.
entries.613e212d7992012879c4703eb6023835b045ed87: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.3-Lev.7.7">Lev 7:3-7</reference> <div eID="gen1228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1229" type="x-p"/> The fat portions only were to be burned upon the altar, viz., the same as in the sin and peace-offerings (see <reference osisRef="Lev.4.8">Lev 4:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.3.9">Lev 3:9</reference>); but the flesh was to be eaten by the priests, as in the sin-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.22">Lev 6:22</reference>), inasmuch as there was the same law in this respect for both the sin-offering and trespass-offering; and these parts of the sacrificial service must therefore have had the same meaning, every trespass being a sin (see <reference osisRef="Lev.6.26">Lev 6:26</reference>). - Certain analogous instructions respecting the burnt-offering and meat-offering are appended in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.8-Lev.7.10">Lev 7:8-10</reference> by way of supplement, as they ought properly to have been given in ch. 6, in the laws relating to the sacrifices in question.
entries.3da1f1f6ae6b0cff1ea9ed846665d96bdb13c484: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.8-Lev.7.10">Lev 7:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen1229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1230" type="x-p"/> In the case of the burnt-offering, the skin of the animal was to fall to the lot of the officiating priest, viz., as payment for his services. הכּהן is construed absolutely: “<hi type="italic">as for the priest, who offereth - the skin of the burnt-offering which he offereth shall belong to the priest</hi>” (for “<hi type="italic">to him</hi>”). This was probably the case also with the trespass-offerings and sin-offerings of the laity; whereas the skin of the peace-offerings belonged to the owner of the animal (see <hi type="italic">Mishnah, Sebach.</hi> 12, 3). - In <reference osisRef="Lev.7.9">Lev 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.10">Lev 7:10</reference>, the following law is laid down with reference to the meat-offering, that everything baked in the oven, and everything prepared in a pot or pan, was to belong to the priest, who burned a portion of it upon the altar; and that everything mixed with oil and everything dry was to belong to all the sons of Aaron, i.e., to all the priests, to one as much as another, so that they were all to receive an equal share. The reason for this distinction is not very clear. That all the meat-offerings described in ch. 2 should fall to the sons of Aaron (i.e., to the priests), with the exception of that portion which was burned upon the altar as an azcarah, followed from the fact that they were most holy (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.2.3">Lev 2:3</reference>). As the meat-offerings, which consisted of pastry, and were offered in the form of prepared food (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.9">Lev 7:9</reference>), are the same as those described in <reference osisRef="Lev.2.4-Lev.2.8">Lev 2:4-8</reference>, it is evident that by those mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.2.10">Lev 2:10</reference> we are to understand the kinds described in <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1-Lev.2.3">Lev 2:1-3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.2.14-Lev.2.16">Lev 2:14-16</reference>, and by the “dry,” primarily the קלוּי אביב, which consisted of dried grains, to which oil was to be added (נתן <reference osisRef="Lev.2.15">Lev 2:15</reference>), though not poured upon it, as in the case of the offering of flour (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Lev 2:1</reference>), and probably also in that of the sin-offerings and jealousy-offerings (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.11">Lev 5:11</reference>, and Num 5:15), which consisted simply of flour (without oil). The reason therefore why those which consisted of cake and pastry fell to the lot of the officiating priest, and those which consisted of flour mixed with oil, of dry corn, or of simple flour, were divided among all the priests, was probably simply this, that the former were for the most part offered only under special circumstances, and then merely in small quantities, whereas the latter were the ordinary forms in which the meat-offerings were presented, and amounted to more than the officiating priests could possibly consume, or dispose of by themselves.
entries.a0ce97b61b06d96a79759d9d64480b2f01a49792: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.11-Lev.7.12">Lev 7:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen1230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1231" type="x-p"/> The Law of the Peace-Offerings, “<hi type="italic">which he shall offer to Jehovah</hi>” (the subject is to be supplied from the verb), contains instructions, (1) as to the bloodless accompaniment to these sacrifices (Lev 7:12-14), (2) as to the eating of the flesh of the sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.15-Lev.7.21">Lev 7:15-21</reference>), with the prohibition against eating fat and blood (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.22-Lev.7.27">Lev 7:22-27</reference>), and (3) as to Jehovah’s share of these sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.28-Lev.7.36">Lev 7:28-36</reference>). - In <reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">Lev 7:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference> three classes of <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi> are mentioned, which differ according to their occasion and design, viz., whether they were brought על־תּודה, upon the ground of praise, i.e., to praise God for blessings received or desired, or as vow-offerings, or thirdly, as freewill-offerings (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>). To (lit., upon, in addition to) the sacrifice of thanksgiving (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">Lev 7:12</reference>, “sacrifice of thanksgiving of his peace-offerings,” <reference osisRef="Lev.7.13">Lev 7:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">Lev 7:15</reference>) they were to present “<hi type="italic">unleavened cakes kneaded with oil, and flat cakes anointed with oil</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.2.4">Lev 2:4</reference>), <hi type="italic">and roasted fine flour</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Lev.6.14">Lev 6:14</reference>) <hi type="italic">mixed as cakes with oil,</hi>” i.e., cakes made of fine flour roasted with oil, and thoroughly kneaded with oil (on the construction, see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §139, 2; <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> §284 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). This last kind of cakes kneaded with oil is also called oil-bread-cake (“a cake of oiled bread,” <reference osisRef="Lev.8.26">Lev 8:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.23">Exo 29:23</reference>), or “cake unleavened, kneaded with oil” (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.2">Exo 29:2</reference>), and probably differed from the former simply in the fact that it was more thoroughly saturated with oil, inasmuch as it was not only made of flour that had been mixed with oil in the kneading, but the flour itself was first of all roasted in oil, and then the dough was moistened still further with oil in the process of kneading.
entries.01bdaf9a4d39a318acfc756b1e483cda3c78defb: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.13-Lev.7.14">Lev 7:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen1231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1232" type="x-p"/> This sacrificial gift the offerer was to present upon, or along with, cakes of leavened bread (round, leavened bread-cakes), and to offer “<hi type="italic">thereof one out of the whole oblation,</hi>” namely, one cake of each of the three kinds mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.12">Lev 7:12</reference>, as a heave-offering for Jehovah, which was to fall to the priest who sprinkled the blood of the peace-offering. According to <reference osisRef="Lev.2.9">Lev 2:9</reference>, an <hi type="italic">azcarah</hi> of the unleavened pastry was burned upon the altar, although this is not specially mentioned here any more than at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.9">Lev 7:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.7.10">Lev 7:10</reference>; whereas none of the leavened bread-cake was placed upon the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.12">Lev 2:12</reference>), but it was simply used as bread for the sacrificial meal. There is nothing here to suggest an allusion to the custom of offering unleavened sacrificial cakes upon a plate of leavened dough, as <hi type="italic">J. D. Michaelis, Winer, </hi>and others suppose.
entries.c49ff92dfdb6ccc56ff50a04021ad0b2923e6c50: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.15-Lev.7.18">Lev 7:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen1232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1233" type="x-p"/> The flesh of the praise-offering was to be eaten on the day of presentation, and none of it was to be left till the next morning (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.22.29-Lev.22.30">Lev 22:29-30</reference>); but that of the vow and freewill-offerings might be eaten on both the first and second days. Whatever remained after that was to be burnt on the third day, i.e., to be destroyed by burning. If any was eaten on the third day, it was not well-pleasing (ירצה “good pleasure,” see <reference osisRef="Lev.1.4">Lev 1:4</reference>), and was “<hi type="italic">not reckoned to the offerer,</hi>” sc., as a sacrifice well-pleasing to God; it was “<hi type="italic">an abomination</hi>.” פּגּוּל, an abomination, is only applied to the flesh of the sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.7">Lev 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.14">Eze 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">Isa 65:4</reference>), and signifies properly a stench; - compare the talmudic word פּגּל <hi type="italic">faetidum reddere</hi>. Whoever ate thereof would bear his sin (see <reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Lev 5:1</reference>). “<hi type="italic">The soul that eateth</hi>” is not to be restricted, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes, to the other participators in the sacrificial meal, but applies to the offerer also, in fact to every one who partook of such flesh. The burning on the third day was commanded, not to compel the offerer to invite the poor to share in the meal (<hi type="italic">Theodoret</hi>, <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi>, etc.), but to guard against the danger of a desecration of the meal. The sacrificial flesh was holy (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.34">Exo 29:34</reference>); and in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.8">Lev 19:8</reference>, where this command is repeated,<note placement="foot">There is no foundation for <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> assertion, that in Lev 19:5. another early lawgiver introduces a milder regulation with regard to the thank-offering, and allows all the thank-offerings to be eaten on the second day. For Lev 19:5. does not profess to lay down a universal rule with regard to all the thank-offerings, but presupposes our law, and simply enforces its regulations with regard to the vow and freewill-offerings, and threatens transgressors with severe punishment.</note> eating it on the third day is called a profanation of that which was holy to Jehovah, and ordered to be punished with extermination. It became a desecration of what was holy, through the fact that in warm countries, if flesh is not most carefully preserved by artificial means, it begins to putrefy, or becomes offensive (פּגּוּל) on the third day. But to eat flesh that was putrid or stinking, would be like eating unclean carrion, or the נבלה with which putrid flesh is associated in Eze 4:14. It was for this reason that burning was commanded, as <hi type="italic">Philo</hi> (<hi type="italic">de vict.</hi> p. 842) and <hi type="italic">Maimonides</hi> (<hi type="italic">More Neboch</hi> iii. 46) admit; though the former also associates with this the purpose mentioned above, which we decidedly reject (cf. <hi type="italic">Outram</hi> l.c. p. 185 seq., and Bähr, ii. pp. 375-6).
entries.19262c1c937819fd535a7f9f7a8cf924c6fb4504: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.19-Lev.7.21">Lev 7:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen1233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1234" type="x-p"/> In the same way all sacrificial flesh that had come into contact with what was unclean, and been defiled in consequence, was to be burned and not eaten. <reference osisRef="Lev.7.19">Lev 7:19</reference>, which is not found in the Septuagint and Vulgate, reads thus: “<hi type="italic">and as for the flesh, every clean person shall eat flesh,</hi>” i.e., take part in the sacrificial meal.
entries.8406f8a6720a645a662c0c1cfa03cff5427232eb: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.22-Lev.7.23">Lev 7:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen1234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1235" type="x-p"/> On the other hand, “<hi type="italic">the soul which eats flesh of the peace-offering, and his uncleanness is upon him</hi> (for “whilst uncleanness is upon him;” the suffix is to be understood as referring to נפשׁ construed as a masculine, see <reference osisRef="Lev.2.1">Lev 2:1</reference>), “<hi type="italic">shall be cut off</hi>” (see <reference osisRef="Gen.17.14">Gen 17:14</reference>). This was to be done, whether the uncleanness arose from contact with an unclean object (any unclean thing), or from the uncleanness of man (cf. ch. 12-15), or from an unclean beast (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.11.4-Lev.11.8">Lev 11:4-8</reference>), or from any other unclean abomination. שׁקץ, abomination, includes the unclean fishes, birds, and smaller animals, to which this expression is applied in <reference osisRef="Lev.11.10-Lev.11.42">Lev 11:10-42</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.10">Eze 8:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.66.17">Isa 66:17</reference>). Moreover contact with animals that were pronounced unclean so far as eating was concerned, did not produce uncleanness so long as they were alive, or if they had been put to death by man; but contact with animals that had died a natural death, whether they belonged to the edible animals or not, that is to say, with carrion (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.11.8">Lev 11:8</reference>). <div eID="gen1235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1236" type="x-p"/> There is appended to these regulations, as being substantially connected with them, the prohibition of fat and blood as articles of food (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.22-Lev.7.27">Lev 7:22-27</reference>). By “<hi type="italic">the fat of ox, or of sheep, or of goat,</hi>” i.e., the three kinds of animals used in sacrifice, or “<hi type="italic">the fat of the beast of which men offer a firing to Jehovah</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.25">Lev 7:25</reference>), we are to understand only those portions of fat which are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Lev.3.3-Lev.3.4">Lev 3:3-4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.3.9">Lev 3:9</reference>; not fat which grows in with the flesh, nor the fat portions of other animals, which were clean but not allowed as sacrifices, such as the stag, the antelope, and other kinds of game.
entries.f4c016951ae4fdaf0a4313c756a3bc9743414bb6: <reference osisRef="Lev.7.24-Lev.7.27">Lev 7:24-27</reference> <div eID="gen1236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1237" type="x-p"/> The fat of cattle that had fallen (נבלה), or been torn to pieces (viz., by beasts of prey), was not to be eaten, because it was unclean and defiled the eater (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.15">Lev 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.22.8">Lev 22:8</reference>); but it might be applied “<hi type="italic">to all kinds of uses,</hi>” i.e., to the common purposes of ordinary life. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> observes on this, that “in the case of oxen, sheep, and goats slain in the regular way, this was evidently not allowable. But the law does not say what was to be done with the fat of these animals.” Certainly it does not <hi type="italic">disertis verbis;</hi> but indirectly it does so clearly enough. According to Lev 17:3., during the journey through the desert any one who wanted to slaughter an ox, sheep, or goat was to bring the animal to the tabernacle as a sacrificial gift, that the blood might be sprinkled against the altar, and the fat burned upon it. By this regulation every ordinary slaughtering was raised into a sacrifice, and the law determined what was to be done with the fat. Now if afterwards, when the people dwelt in Canaan, cattle were allowed to be slaughtered in any place, and the only prohibition repeated was that against eating blood (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.15-Deut.12.16">Deu 12:15-16</reference>, Deu 12:21.), whilst the law against eating fat was not renewed; it follows as a matter of course, that when the custom of slaughtering at the tabernacle was restricted to actual sacrifices, the prohibition against eating the fat portions came to an end, so far as those animals were concerned with were slain for consumption and not as sacrifices. The reason for prohibiting fat from being eaten was simply this, that so long as every slaughtering was a sacrifice, the fat portions, which were to be handed over to Jehovah and burned upon the altar, were not to be devoted to earthly purposes, because they were gifts sanctified to God. The eating of the fat, therefore, was neither prohibited on sanitary or social grounds, viz., because fat was injurious to health, as <hi type="italic">Maimonides</hi> and other Rabbins maintain, nor for the purpose of promoting the cultivation of olives, as <hi type="italic">Michaelis</hi> supposes, nor to prevent its being put into the unclean mouth of man, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> imagines; but as being an illegal appropriation of what was sanctified to God, a wicked invasion of the rights of Jehovah, which was to be punished with extermination according to the analogy of Num 15:30-31. The prohibition of blood in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.26">Lev 7:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.27">Lev 7:27</reference>, extends to birds and cattle; fishes not being mentioned, because the little blood which they possess is not generally eaten.
